source: A physical change (cutting, melting, dissolving) keeps the same substance. A chemical change makes a new substance: signs are a gas, a new color, light, heat or a smell.
Thinking melting is a chemical change because the ice "turns into something else". Melted ice is still water; burning wood is a chemical change because ash and smoke are new substances.
Cut paper, melt butter or dissolve sugar, and you still have paper, butter and sugar. Burn paper or bake a cake, and you get something new.
A physical change changes size, shape or state, but it is still the same substance. A chemical change makes a new substance.
Signs of a chemical change: bubbles of a new gas, a new color, light or heat given off, or a new smell. (Bubbles alone are not proof: boiling water bubbles too.)
Signs that something new has formed.
An apple slice turns brown after an hour on the counter. Physical or chemical?
It formed because the apple reacted with oxygen in the air.
Calling melting a chemical change. Melted ice is still water and can freeze again. A burnt piece of toast cannot be turned back into bread.
In any change, the total mass stays the same if nothing escapes. When baking soda fizzes in vinegar in an open cup, the cup gets lighter because the gas floats away.
Going further. Try mixing safely on screen in the Mixing Lab. Michael Faraday's The Chemical History of a Candle is a classic for older readers.
